[package]
name = "matrix-rtc-call-sdk"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
publish = false
description = "The call SDK hosts use: the call's media over any transport (participants, tiles, the unified event stream, the call engine), attaching it to a joined call, and the native LiveKit facade."

[dependencies]
matrix-rtc-core = { path = "../matrix-rtc-core" }
# The transport contract the engine drives, and the key handler `attach` installs.
matrix-rtc-transport = { path = "../matrix-rtc-transport" }
# The joined `RtcCall` media attaches to, and the call types the engine merges
# onto its roster (raised hands, reactions).
matrix-rtc-call = { path = "../matrix-rtc-call" }
# The engine's actor loop multiplexes channels with `tokio::select!`
# (`macros`). Tasks and timers go through `matrix_rtc_core::executor`.
tokio = { workspace = true, features = ["macros"] }
# `join_all`, so a batched stats read awaits every track at once (`alloc`).
futures-util = { version = "0.3", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
async-trait.workspace = true
log.workspace = true
thiserror.workspace = true

# --- `livekit` feature: native LiveKit media (pulls libwebrtc) ---------------
matrix-rtc-livekit = { path = "../matrix-rtc-livekit", optional = true }
# The types `matrix-rtc-livekit`'s API names that the facade and examples use
# too (`RoomEvent`, the token exchange's `reqwest::Client`); the workspace's
# specs, so they are the same crates.
livekit = { workspace = true, optional = true }
reqwest = { workspace = true, optional = true }

# --- `matrix-sdk` feature: the `LiveKitCall` facade over matrix-rust-sdk -----
# `SdkMatrixBackend`, the matrix-rust-sdk `MatrixBackend` the facade drives.
# Nothing in it knows about LiveKit.
matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk = { path = "../matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk", optional = true }
# The facade takes a `matrix_sdk::Room`. Everything else Matrix-side is
# `matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk`'s, and the rationale for the feature set (why room-key
# forwarding stays on, what `experimental-send-custom-to-device` is for) lives
# there, next to the code that depends on it. The rev is the workspace's, so the
# two crates cannot drift onto two copies of matrix-sdk.
matrix-sdk = { workspace = true, optional = true, features = ["experimental-send-custom-to-device"] }
# Drives sliding sync plus the encryption sync in the examples and the e2e test.
# Its `unstable-msc4354` (enabled by our `matrix-sdk` feature) turns on the
# sliding-sync sticky-events extension, so sticky events actually flow;
# encryption support rides along via matrix-sdk's default features.
matrix-sdk-ui = { workspace = true, optional = true }

[features]
# Native LiveKit media: `attach_livekit`. Off by default — it pulls the LiveKit
# client and libwebrtc; the web binding brings its own transport and uses none.
livekit = ["dep:matrix-rtc-livekit", "dep:livekit", "dep:reqwest"]
# The `LiveKitCall` join/leave facade over a `matrix_sdk::Client`, its examples
# and `e2e_call`. Off by default to keep the crate buildable without the git
# SDK. `matrix-sdk-ui/unstable-msc4354` is what makes `SyncService` request
# sticky events over sliding sync.
matrix-sdk = [
    "livekit",
    "dep:matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk",
    "dep:matrix-sdk",
    "dep:matrix-sdk-ui",
    "matrix-sdk-ui/unstable-msc4354",
]
# The LiveKit tone generator and frequency detector, for the examples and
# integration tests. Also turns on matrix-sdk's `testing`, whose only use here
# is `Client::olm_machine_for_testing` — the one public route to the
# `OlmMachine`, and so the only way to reach `set_room_key_forwarding_enabled`.
# It costs `wiremock` and friends in the graph, which is what a testing feature
# is for.
testing = ["matrix-rtc-livekit?/testing", "matrix-sdk?/testing"]

# The end-to-end call test (see tests/E2E_CALL.md). `required-features` keeps
# plain `cargo test --workspace` from compiling it (and the git SDK + libwebrtc
# behind it); the `#[ignore]` inside keeps `--all-features` runs from executing
# it without the demo/backend stack.
[[test]]
name = "e2e_call"
path = "tests/e2e_call/main.rs"
required-features = ["matrix-sdk", "testing"]

[dev-dependencies]
# `MockBackend`, to join a real call in the `attach` tests.
matrix-rtc-core = { path = "../matrix-rtc-core", features = ["testing"] }
# `MediaStatusReporter::standalone`, to watch what the engine reports.
matrix-rtc-call = { path = "../matrix-rtc-call", features = ["testing"] }
serde = { workspace = true }
serde_json.workspace = true
# `signal` for the join_and_record example's Ctrl-C hang-up; `io-std` for the
# interop_peer example, which is driven over stdin by the Playwright suite.
tokio = { version = "1", features = [
  "rt",
  "rt-multi-thread",
  "macros",
  "time",
  "sync",
  "test-util",
  "signal",
  "io-std",
  "io-util",
] }
futures-util = "0.3"
futures-core = "0.3"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter"] }
# Argument parsing for the `load_test` example. A dev-dependency on purpose:
# examples may use them, so clap never enters the library's dependency graph.
clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive", "env"] }
# The dependency tree pulls in rustls with BOTH the `ring` and `aws-lc-rs`
# crypto backends (livekit/reqwest vs matrix-sdk), so rustls cannot pick a
# process-level `CryptoProvider` automatically and panics on first TLS use. The
# examples install `aws-lc-rs` explicitly (matches matrix-sdk's default); this
# dev-dep gives us the provider module to call `install_default()`.
rustls = { version = "0.23", features = ["aws_lc_rs"] }

[[example]]
name = "connect"
required-features = ["matrix-sdk"]

# The quick-start example (see README.md). `testing` only for the optional
# PUBLISH_TONE test-tone publisher, so two instances can call each other.
[[example]]
name = "join_and_record"
required-features = ["matrix-sdk", "testing"]

# The Rust half of the Element Call interop test (see interop/README.md and
# demo/backend/INTEROP.md). Driven over stdin by Playwright, which owns the
# browser running Element Call. `testing` for the tone generator it publishes
# so Element Call has media to render.
[[example]]
name = "interop_peer"
required-features = ["matrix-sdk", "testing"]

# The layered client → room → call flow publishing a video file (see README.md).
[[example]]
name = "publish_video"
required-features = ["matrix-sdk"]

# The load generator (see README.md). Publishes a video file from N devices of
# one account. `testing` is only for `Client::olm_machine_for_testing`, used to
# keep room-key gossip out of the to-device traffic this tool measures.
[[example]]
name = "load_test"
required-features = ["matrix-sdk", "testing"]

[package]
name = "matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
publish = false
description = "The matrix-rust-sdk implementation of the MatrixRTC core's MatrixBackend."

[lib]
crate-type = ["rlib"]

[dependencies]
matrix-rtc-core = { path = "../matrix-rtc-core" }
serde = { workspace = true }
serde_json = { workspace = true }
async-trait.workspace = true
log.workspace = true

# The per-subscription tasks and their wake/retry timers; the SDK brings the
# runtime.
tokio = { workspace = true }

# Upstream matrix-rust-sdk (rev in the workspace manifest). Keeps its default
# features (e2e-encryption, sqlite, rustls-aws-lc-rs,
# automatic-room-key-forwarding). See `sdk`.
#
# Key forwarding stays ON deliberately. Without it a freshly logged-in device
# cannot obtain the Megolm sessions for member events sent before it existed,
# and simply does not see those peers — the exact failure that makes an
# in-progress Element Call invisible to a new device. Tools that want the
# request/forward chatter out of their measurements switch it off per client at
# runtime instead; see `matrix-rtc-call-sdk/examples/load_test.rs`.
#
# `experimental-send-custom-to-device` exposes
# `Encryption::encrypt_and_send_raw_to_device`, used to distribute MSC4143 media
# keys as Olm-encrypted to-device messages (see `sdk`). It pulls in
# `e2e-encryption`, already on via defaults.
#
# `unstable-msc4354` for MSC4354 sticky events, the spec-current membership
# carrier. Their `encryption_info().sender_device` is the only source for a
# member event's sending device now that MSC4143 has dropped
# `member.claimed_device_id`. See `sdk::snapshot`.
#
# Member events are parsed with `matrix_rtc_core::RawStickyEventContent`, never
# ruma's typed RTC events: upstream ruma does not model the 2026 MSC4143 rewrite,
# and the core must not depend on ruma anyway.
matrix-sdk = { workspace = true, features = ["experimental-send-custom-to-device", "unstable-msc4354"] }
# Only needed to name `crypto::CollectStrategy` (the key-sharing strategy passed
# to `encrypt_and_send_raw_to_device`); matrix-sdk does not re-export it.
# `e2e-encryption` gates the `crypto` re-export.
matrix-sdk-base = { workspace = true, features = ["e2e-encryption"] }

[dev-dependencies]
matrix-rtc-core = { path = "../matrix-rtc-core", features = ["testing"] }
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt", "rt-multi-thread", "macros", "test-util", "time", "sync"] }

# matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk

The matrix-rust-sdk implementation of `matrix-rtc-core`'s `MatrixBackend`. The
core (which also holds the feeder) and the call layer (`matrix-rtc-call`, which
also holds the pre-2026 Element Call dialects) drive any backend; this crate is the one over a
`matrix_sdk::Client`. It is deliberately **transport-free** — nothing in it
knows what a LiveKit SFU is.

## Module map

| Module | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`sdk`** | `SdkMatrixBackend` implements `MatrixBackend` over a `matrix_sdk::Client`: Client-Server requests for the sends, and for the reads a task per room subscription that delivers the complete current sets on subscribe and again on every sticky-store or room-state wake, plus the to-device handlers, `/relations`, the OpenID token and `GET /rtc/transports`. |

## Testing

```sh
cargo test -p matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk
```

# matrix-rtc-call-sdk

The call SDK hosts use: a call's media over any transport, attached to a call
joined through `matrix-rtc-call`.

- The roster (`Participant`s keyed by `member_id`), the tiles a UI draws, the
  unified `CallEvent` stream, and the `CallEngine` that builds them over
  `matrix-rtc-transport`'s MSC4195 multi-focus connection pool, for any
  transport.
- `attach_media`, the one wiring of media onto a joined `RtcCall`.
- Behind `livekit`: `attach_livekit`, the native LiveKit transport
  (`matrix-rtc-livekit`) attached to a call.
- Behind `matrix-sdk`: `LiveKitCall`, a join/leave facade over a
  `matrix_sdk::Client`, plus the examples and the end-to-end test.

Without features it compiles for wasm32 and pulls neither libwebrtc nor
matrix-sdk; the web binding uses it so. The FFI takes `livekit`.

## Quick start: join a call and record

With the `matrix-sdk` feature, [`LiveKitCall::join`](src/livekit/call.rs) wraps the whole
stack — MSC4143 membership signalling (via MSC4354 sticky events), media-key
exchange over Olm-encrypted to-device messages, the MSC4195 token exchange,
and an E2EE-enabled SFU connection — in one handle:

```rust,no_run
use std::time::Duration;
use matrix_rtc_call_sdk::{LiveKitCall, LiveKitCallOptions};
use livekit::{RoomEvent, track::RemoteTrack};
use matrix_rtc_livekit::media;
use matrix_sdk_ui::sync_service::SyncService;

async fn record_a_call() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // A logged-in, syncing client that has joined the call's room.
    let client = matrix_sdk::Client::builder()
        .homeserver_url("http://localhost:8008")
        .build()
        .await?;
    client.matrix_auth().login_username("bob", "secret").send().await?;
    let sync = SyncService::builder(client.clone()).build().await?;
    sync.start().await;

    let room = client.get_room("!room:example.org".try_into()?).unwrap();

    // Join: membership + key exchange + E2EE SFU connection.
    let mut call = LiveKitCall::join(&room, LiveKitCallOptions::default()).await?;

    // React to the LiveKit event stream: record the first audio track.
    while let Some(event) = call.events().recv().await {
        if let RoomEvent::TrackSubscribed { track: RemoteTrack::Audio(audio), .. } = event {
            let pcm = media::record_track(&audio, Duration::from_secs(5)).await;
            media::write_wav("call.wav", &pcm, media::SAMPLE_RATE)?;
            break;
        }
    }

    call.leave().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Two things the snippet glosses over:

- **Runtime.** `LiveKitCall::join` spawns the call's background work onto the current
  tokio runtime, so it must run inside one:

  ```rust,no_run
  fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
      // Two rustls crypto backends end up in the dependency tree
      // (livekit → ring, matrix-sdk → aws-lc-rs); pick one explicitly.
      rustls::crypto::aws_lc_rs::default_provider().install_default().unwrap();

      let runtime = tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread().enable_all().build()?;
      runtime.block_on(record_a_call())
  }
  ```

- **An open slot.** MSC4143 counts nobody as joined against a closed slot; the
  room creator opens one with `matrix_rtc_call_sdk::open_slot(...)` (see the
  example below).

- **When the loop ends.** The event stream ending *is* the "call is over"
  signal: the channel closes on `leave()` and after any unrecoverable
  disconnect (a `RoomEvent::Disconnected` with the reason arrives first;
  transient drops auto-resume and don't end the stream). What the stream does
  **not** have is a deadline — if no peer ever publishes, the loop above waits
  forever, so a real bot should wrap the wait in `tokio::time::timeout`.

The runnable version is [`examples/join_and_record.rs`](examples/join_and_record.rs) —
it adds slot opening and an optional test-tone publisher, so **two instances of
it can call each other** against the local [`demo/backend`](../../demo/backend/README.md)
stack:

```sh
make backend-up   # from the repo root

# terminal 1: publish a tone
MX_USER=alice MX_PASSWORD=secret ROOM_ID='!room:synapse' OPEN_SLOT=1 PUBLISH_TONE=1 \
cargo run -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --example join_and_record --features matrix-sdk,testing

# terminal 2: record it
MX_USER=bob MX_PASSWORD=secret ROOM_ID='!room:synapse' \
cargo run -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --example join_and_record --features matrix-sdk,testing
```

(Register the users and create the room as described in the
[`demo/backend` README](../../demo/backend/README.md). The MSC4153
cross-signing requirement stays at the core's default: each user's first run
bootstraps cross-signing and prints a **recovery key**, and since every run
logs in a fresh device, subsequent runs need that key passed as
`RECOVERY_KEY=...` so the new device gets cross-signed.)

## Load testing

[`examples/load_test.rs`](examples/load_test.rs) drives a deployment with N
virtual participants: it logs in N devices of **one** account, walks them
through the same join sequence a real client uses, and has each publish a video
file as its camera track. Run it while watching the same call in Element Web to
inspect SFU/homeserver/client behaviour.

The easiest way in is
[`scripts/load-test-sample.sh`](../../scripts/load-test-sample.sh): copy it,
fill in the block at the top once, then run your copy. `scripts/load-test.sh`
is git-ignored, so the password and recovery key in it stay out of the
repository. Extra flags pass straight through and win over the block, so
one-off tweaks need no edit:

```sh
cp scripts/load-test-sample.sh scripts/load-test.sh
$EDITOR scripts/load-test.sh
./scripts/load-test.sh                               # your defaults
./scripts/load-test.sh --devices 10 --no-simulcast   # one-off override
```

Or invoke it directly:

```sh
cargo run --release -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --example load_test \
    --features matrix-sdk -- \
    --user loadtest --password secret --recovery-key 'EsT ...' \
    --room '!room:synapse' --video clip.mp4 --devices 5
```

Every argument also reads from an environment variable (`MX_USER`,
`MX_PASSWORD`, `RECOVERY_KEY`, `ROOM_ID`, `HOMESERVER_URL`) — prefer that for
the secrets. `--help` lists the rest; the ones that matter most are
`--resolution` / `--fps` / `--clip-seconds`, `--audio`, `--subscribe`, and the
`--ramp-ms` / `--login-delay-ms` pacing.

Notes:

- **`ffmpeg` must be on `PATH`**, unless the input is already `.y4m` or raw
  `.yuv`. It is invoked once at startup to decode `--clip-seconds` of the file
  into memory; every device then loops that same buffer from a different
  offset. One shared decode keeps the CPU going into encoding, which is what
  the run is meant to exercise.
- **The recovery key is required.** Each device is a fresh login, and neither
  the SDK's identity-based to-device strategy nor the core's MSC4153 policy
  will exchange media keys with a device that is not cross-signed.
- **`--store <folder>` reuses devices between runs.** Device *i* keeps its
  session and sqlite crypto store in `<folder>/device-i`; a run restores what is
  there and only logs in for the devices that are missing. Two payoffs: repeat
  runs pay no login cost at all (so the `--login-delay-ms` rate limiting above
  stops mattering), and a restored device keeps its Megolm sessions, so it can
  decrypt member events sent *before* the run started — a fresh device cannot,
  which is why a peer already in the call can stay invisible to it until they
  re-join. Implies `--keep-devices`, since logging out would revoke the stored
  token; `--purge-devices` clears the folder along with the devices.
- **The room must be encrypted.** A member event's sending device is only known
  from its decryption metadata, so in a cleartext room memberships cannot be
  mapped to media at all. The tool warns and continues.
- **Devices are removed on exit** (a plain logout per device). A run killed
  with `kill -9` leaves them behind; `--purge-devices` deletes every device
  whose display name carries `--device-prefix` and exits.
- **`--sticky-duration-ms` defaults to 2 minutes here, against the library's
  one hour.** A run that is killed rather than left cleanly leaves its
  memberships standing until this elapses: the dead man's switch does *not*
  clear them, because its delayed leave is a plain event that never replaces
  the sticky entry. An hour of ghost participants makes the next attempt
  useless. The cost is one extra membership send per device every half of it,
  and it must stay well above twice the 10 s keep-alive or memberships lapse
  between ticks.
- **Scale is bounded by your machine, not the SFU** — see
  [How many devices?](#how-many-devices) below.
- Devices join publish-only by default (`LiveKitCallOptions::auto_subscribe = false`).
  `--subscribe` makes them decode every peer as a real client would, at N×N
  cost.
- **Keep simulcast on when a real client is watching.** `--no-simulcast`
  publishes a single encoding with no rid, so the SFU advertises no layers to
  choose from. A subscriber using adaptive stream (Element Call, Element Web,
  any livekit-client app) asks for a specific layer, that request resolves to
  nothing, and no video is forwarded — a grey tile with *no* decryption errors,
  since no frames arrive at all. Audio still works, which makes it look like an
  E2EE fault when it isn't. Reserve `--no-simulcast` for scale runs where
  nobody renders the participants.
- N devices of one account is equivalent to N accounts here: membership is keyed
  on a random per-join `member_id`, the MSC4195 identity hashes
  `(user, device, member_id)`, and the core distributes media keys to other
  devices of our own user like any other peer.
- **Sharing the call with Element Call** (the JS SDK, which still speaks a
  pre-2026 MatrixRTC format) needs `--format sticky` /
  `LEGACY_ELEMENT_CALL=sticky`, plus `--open-slot`: that client publishes no
  `m.rtc.slot`, and a slot nobody opened reads as closed, which projects every
  member out of the call. Media keys then go out under the legacy to-device type
  *instead of* the spec one, so such a run exchanges keys with Element Call or
  with spec-current peers, never both. Reading that format needs no flag.
  For a build older still — membership as `org.matrix.msc3401.call.member` room
  state — use `state` instead of `sticky`, and leave `--open-slot` off: that
  generation has no slot concept. See `matrix_rtc_core::compat`.

Homeservers with rate limiting may reject a burst of logins or messages;
`--login-delay-ms` and `--ramp-ms` space them out. **Past 3 devices this is not
optional against a stock Synapse**: `rc_login` defaults to `per_second: 0.17,
burst_count: 3`, so the first three logins go through and the rest need ~6 s
each. Exceeding it returns 429 `Too many login attempts`. The tool waits that
out — five attempts per device with doubling backoff, honouring the server's
`retry_after` when it sends one — so a run survives a limiter it outruns, but
pacing it properly is faster than being throttled into it. Use
`--login-delay-ms 7000` or more for double-digit device counts; only a
homeserver you control (`demo/backend` sets every `rc_*` to 1000/1000)
tolerates the tighter default. Errors that are not rate limiting — a wrong
password, an unreachable homeserver — still fail on the first attempt.

### How many devices?

**Short answer: start at 5, double until the stats line sags, and stay one
step below that.** The numbers below are derived from the code, not measured —
treat them as a starting point, and the stats line as the truth.

The binding constraint is almost always **video encoding on the machine
running the tool**. Every device is a separate peer connection with its own
encoder set (the LiveKit Rust SDK has no publish-pre-encoded path), and how
many encoders that is depends on resolution and simulcast —
`compute_video_encodings` in livekit `src/room/options.rs`:

| `--resolution` | simulcast on | simulcast off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 320x240 (long edge < 480) | 1 | 1 |
| 640x360 *(default)* | 2 | 1 |
| 1280x720 | 3 | 1 |

So 10 devices at 640x360 is 20 concurrent VP8 encoders with simulcast on, or
10 with `--no-simulcast` (which the sample script sets). As a rough budget,
one encoder per available core is a sane place to begin — a modern laptop
running the sample script's defaults (640x360, 15 fps, no simulcast) should
manage somewhere in the low tens; with simulcast on, halve it; at 720p with
simulcast, halve it again. `--subscribe` adds N×N decoding on top and cuts
whatever you land on by a lot.

**The measurement that settles it** is the health line printed every 10 s:

```
  [0] 150 frames/10s, 900 total, 0 errors, 4 members
```

While `frames/10s` stays near `--fps × 10`, every device is really publishing
at the rate you asked for. Once it drops, the generator is saturated: the
extra devices are not producing the load you think they are, and any
server-side number you read from that run is understating things. That is the
point to stop adding devices and instead run a second process, or a second
machine.

Two ceilings that are *not* about your CPU, and that you may actually want to
hit deliberately:

- **Media-key distribution is quadratic.** Keys go out as individually
  Olm-encrypted to-device messages, one per recipient device — bringing up N
  devices costs O(N²) messages. Teardown is worse: the core rotates the key
  whenever anyone leaves (`matrix-rtc-core/src/encryption/mod.rs`), so each
  departure makes every survivor re-key and re-send. With a few dozen devices
  the leave storm at shutdown is heavier than the join ramp was. If the
  homeserver struggles at the *end* of a run rather than during it, this is
  why.
- **One sliding-sync connection per device**, all for the same account, plus N
  logins during setup. `--login-delay-ms` and `--ramp-ms` pace the setup; the
  steady-state syncs are unpaced.

# `e2e_call` — end-to-end MatrixRTC/LiveKit test (two Rust clients)

An integration test that drives the **whole Rust MatrixRTC stack** end to end —
no browser, no microphone. The flow mirrors setting up a real call from scratch:
`alice` **creates an encrypted room and invites** `bob`, `bob` **joins**, and only
once the two-member room membership has settled do both peers join the same
MatrixRTC slot, discover each other through MSC4354 sticky events, exchange
per-participant media keys over encrypted to-device messages, connect to the
LiveKit SFU **with per-participant frame E2EE enabled**, and prove real media:
`alice` publishes a 440 Hz tone, `bob` decrypts what the SFU forwards and verifies
the frequency.

It is `#[ignore]`-gated because it needs the `demo/backend` docker stack; CI
runs it on every PR (`.github/workflows/e2e-call.yml`).

Source: [`e2e_call/main.rs`](./e2e_call/main.rs) (flow) and
[`e2e_call/provision.rs`](./e2e_call/provision.rs) (throwaway-user
registration).

## What it proves

| Layer | What's exercised |
| --- | --- |
| **Room setup** | `alice` creates an **encrypted** room (`m.room.encryption`) with `shared` history visibility and invites `bob`; `bob` joins; both wait for the 2-member membership before any RTC signalling. |
| **Signalling** | Each client publishes its own `m.rtc.member` membership as a sticky event (+ a dead-man's-switch delayed leave) and discovers the peer via `sticky_events().subscribe()` → the call crate's feeder → the room. Both peers join the room before RTC signalling. Success = each side sees 2 members. |
| **Transport** | MSC4195 OpenID→JWT token exchange and SFU connect for both clients. |
| **Encryption** | The core `EncryptionManager` generates a per-participant media key and distributes it to the peer as an Olm-encrypted `m.rtc.encryption_key` to-device message (`SdkMatrixBackend::send_to_device_message`). Each side imports received keys into its LiveKit `KeyProvider` (`MediaKeyBridge`), addressed by the MSC4195 pseudonymous identity. Success = `bob` imported `alice`'s key. |
| **Media** | 440 Hz tone published by `alice`, **GCM frame-encrypted** at the SFU, decrypted and recorded by `bob`, verified with a Goertzel filter (`media::detect_tone > 0.5`). A WAV is written to `target/e2e/received-<label>.wav` — inside the repo, not the system temp dir — and uploaded as a CI artifact on failure. A scenario that records twice (the redial) keeps both files. The tone only decodes because the keys were exchanged and mapped correctly. |
| **Multi-SFU** (`e2e_call_two_foci_*`) | The same flow with `alice` publishing on SFU 1 and `bob` on SFU 2 (the backend stack runs two SFU + lk-jwt pairs). Each client's `CallEngine` reads the peer's `transports` from their membership and opens a second connection to the peer's focus (MSC4195 multi-SFU). Tones flow in **both directions** (alice 440 Hz, bob 660 Hz) and are received through the transport-agnostic media API (`LiveKitCall::participants` → `LiveKitCall::remote_track` → frame streams) instead of raw LiveKit events. |
| **Video + constraints** (same scenario) | `alice` publishes a synthetic half-bright/half-dark I420 pattern through `LiveKitCall::publish` (camera track, simulcast + dynacast); `bob` receives it via `video_frames()` across the SFUs and verifies the luma split (robust to VP8 compression). Then `bob` exercises both constraint demand states: `visible = false` **pauses** the stream (frames stop, subscription kept — `set_enabled(false)`) and `visible = true` resumes it instantly; `enabled = false` turns it **off** (released as fully as the transport supports — LiveKit currently pauses here too, because its client-side resubscribe is unreliable at 0.7.48) and `enabled = true` brings frames back. |

## How it's wired

Each participant is a `matrix_rtc_call_sdk::LiveKitCall` (`src/livekit/call.rs`) — the crate's
join/leave facade, so the test exercises exactly what a consumer would use.
Inside `LiveKitCall::join`:

```
matrix_sdk::Client ──login──▶ SyncService (sliding sync; sticky ext auto-on)
        │
        ▼
 SdkMatrixBackend (matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk: src/sdk.rs) — the one MatrixBackend
   sends: sticky / delayed / state / to-device (Olm)      reads: subscribe_room, subscribe_to_device,
        ▲                                                        relations, openid_token, rtc_transports
        │ DialectBackend (compat routing)                        │ complete current sets, on subscribe
        │                                                        ▼ and on every sticky / state wake
 RtcClient → RtcRoom ◀── RoomFeeder / ToDeviceFeeder (core: src/feeder) ── executor::spawn
   └─ join_call → RtcCall (own membership sticky + delayed leave; upkeep)
        │  └─ EncryptionManager: generates + distributes per-participant keys
        │        via the backend's send_to_device_message
        │  └─ MediaKeyBridge (src/keys.rs): received keys ──▶ LiveKit KeyProvider
        ▼                          ▲ (keyed by MSC4195 pseudonymous identity)
 matrix_rtc_livekit::connect_e2ee(..., key_provider) ──▶ LiveKitSession (GCM frame E2EE)
                                            └─ publish_tone / record_track (src/media.rs)
```

The test runs on a multi-thread tokio runtime, with a 300 s overall timeout so
a wedged stack fails fast.

## Prerequisites

The `demo/backend` stack (Synapse + LiveKit SFU + `lk-jwt` auth service).
**Element Web is not needed** — the two Rust clients are each other's peer, and
users, room, and slot are all created at runtime.

```sh
make backend-up
```

## Dependency caveat (important)

The workspace depends on **upstream `matrix-org/matrix-rust-sdk`** (rev in the
root `Cargo.toml`) with its `unstable-msc4354` feature, which our `matrix-sdk`
feature turns on.

Member events go through `matrix_rtc_core::RawStickyEventContent` and
`m.rtc.encryption_key` to-device messages through a raw handler in `call.rs`,
never ruma's typed RTC events: upstream ruma does not model the 2026 MSC4143
rewrite, and the core cannot depend on ruma.

The root `Cargo.toml` also carries the SDK's own `[patch]` blocks (cargo doesn't
propagate a git dep's patches to the consumer).

## Build & run

First build is long (it compiles `matrix-sdk` + native `libwebrtc`).

```sh

cargo test -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --features matrix-sdk,testing \
  --test e2e_call -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

That's the whole invocation against a local `make backend-up` stack — every
setting has a matching default, and two throwaway users (`alice-<run>` /
`bob-<run>`) are registered on the fly, so a persistent `data/` dir never causes
collisions. Overrides for pointing at another deployment:

| Env var | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HOMESERVER_URL` | `http://localhost:8008` | Synapse CS-API base URL |
| `LIVEKIT_SERVICE_URL` | `http://localhost:6080` | `lk-jwt` `/get_token` base URL, pinned via `LiveKitCallOptions::livekit_transport` (overrides the homeserver's MSC4143 transports endpoint) |
| `SLOT_ID` | `m.call#room` | MatrixRTC slot |
| `ALICE` / `ALICE_PW`, `BOB` / `BOB_PW` | *(auto-provisioned)* | Use pre-existing users instead of registering throwaways (for stacks with closed registration) |
| `INSECURE_TLS` | *(unset)* | set (any value) to accept self-signed certs on a remote TLS stack |
| `RUST_LOG` | `info` | tracing filter |

## Notes / troubleshooting

- **Benign log noise.** `matrix_sdk::latest_events…: Failed to deserialize the event`
  (`missing field slot_id`, `CallMemberEventContent` variant mismatch, `missing field
  m.call.id`) and `event_cache…: missing target event id from the redaction event`
  come from the SDK's room-preview builder failing to type legacy/RTC member events.
  They don't touch the sticky path. Quiet them with
  `RUST_LOG=matrix_sdk::latest_events=off,matrix_sdk::event_cache=off`.
- **macOS.** `build.rs` passes `-ObjC` to the linker for examples *and tests* so
  libwebrtc's Objective-C categories aren't dead-stripped (otherwise it aborts at
  runtime with `+[NSString stringForAbslStringView:]: unrecognized selector`). If
  that ever produces duplicate-symbol link errors, switch to `-force_load <libwebrtc.a>`.
- **`room … did not sync within 30s`** — the freshly created room (or `bob`'s
  invite) hasn't come down sliding sync yet; usually a transient re-run fixes it.
- **Registration 500 (`M_UNKNOWN` Internal Server Error) / requests hanging
  mid-test** — synapse's sqlite hit `disk I/O error` (check
  `make backend-logs`). Historically caused by the DB living on a Docker
  Desktop bind mount; it now lives in a named volume, so
  `make backend-down && make backend-up` gives a fresh homeserver. If you see
  this on a checkout that still bind-mounts `./data/synapse`, run
  `make backend-reset`. A wedged homeserver also explains a `leave timed out`
  teardown: RTC sends are bounded (15 s × 3 attempts) so they error out
  instead of hanging forever.
- **Stale `Cargo.lock`** resolving crates.io `matrix-sdk 0.18` → run
  `cargo update -p matrix-sdk`.

## Current limitations / follow-ups

- In the single-focus scenario media is **subscribe-only on the receiver**
  (only `alice` publishes; `bob` records) and verified over the raw LiveKit
  event stream. The two-foci scenario exercises both directions through the
  media API; migrating the single-focus scenario off the raw accessors (and
  deleting them) is the remaining step.
- `receive_encryption_key` fans a received key out to every session in the room
  (the MSC4143 key content carries no `slot_id`); exact for one slot per room.
- The dead-man's-switch delayed leave is a *plain* (non-sticky) delayed event, so
  crash cleanup currently relies on the join sticky's TTL rather than the disconnect
  superseding it — making the delayed leave sticky is a TODO.

name: Lint

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  license-headers:
    name: License headers
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check dual-license headers
        run: ./scripts/check-license-headers.sh

  fmt:
    name: Rustfmt
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt

      # rustfmt only parses source, so it needs no C++ toolchain and can cover
      # the whole workspace, including matrix-rtc-livekit.
      - name: Check formatting
        run: cargo fmt --all --check

  clippy:
    name: Clippy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: clippy

      # matrix-rtc-livekit pulls in livekit/webrtc-sys. Its build script runs
      # even under `cargo clippy` (to generate cxx bindings and link flags) and
      # shells out to pkg-config for glib-2.0, which the prebuilt linux
      # libwebrtc dynamically links. ubuntu-latest ships a C++ toolchain but not
      # libglib2.0-dev, so install it here.
      - name: Install webrtc-sys system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libglib2.0-dev

      # Covers the whole workspace, including matrix-rtc-livekit. Note this
      # does NOT cover matrix-rtc-wasm, whose body is cfg-gated to wasm32 (its
      # JS-backed futures are !Send, so it cannot compile on a host target) —
      # the `wasm` job below is what checks it.
      #
      # `matrix-sdk` + `testing` so the SDK-backed half (`call`, and
      # matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk through it) is type-checked on every PR; without them those modules are not
      # compiled at all.
      - name: Run clippy
        run: >
          cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
          --features matrix-rtc-call-sdk/matrix-sdk,matrix-rtc-call-sdk/testing
          -- -D warnings

  wasm:
    name: Clippy (wasm32)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # matrix-rtc-wasm compiles to an empty crate on any other target, so a
      # host-target clippy run says nothing about it. Everything in it — and the
      # `?Send` half of the core's command traits — is only ever type-checked
      # here.
      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: clippy
          targets: wasm32-unknown-unknown

      - name: Run clippy
        run: >
          cargo clippy -p matrix-rtc-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
          --all-targets -- -D warnings

      # The shared layers a browser build sits on. Lib only (no --all-targets):
      # their test suites are native (tokio `rt-multi-thread`/`time` dev-deps)
      # and neither builds nor runs on wasm32.
      - name: Run clippy (shared crates)
        run: >
          cargo clippy -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk -p matrix-rtc-call
          -p matrix-rtc-transport
          --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -- -D warnings

      # The crate's wasm-bindgen tests, under node: the only place the
      # wasm-only paths (JS command dispatch, the Date.now()-backed clock on
      # the join path) actually execute.
      - name: Install wasm-pack
        run: curl https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-pack/installer/init.sh -sSf | sh

      - name: Run wasm-bindgen tests
        run: wasm-pack test --node crates/matrix-rtc-wasm

name: Element Call interop

on:
  schedule:
    # Catches drift the pins cannot: Element Web and Element Call move daily.
    - cron: "20 4 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled]

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  COMPOSE_FILES: -f demo/backend/docker-compose.yml -f demo/backend/docker-compose.interop.yml

jobs:
  interop:
    name: Rust client vs Element Call
    # Skip PRs that are not asking for it. Scheduled and manual runs always go.
    if: >-
      github.event_name != 'pull_request' ||
      contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'interop')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Generous for the same reason as the E2E Call workflow: an uncached build
    # of matrix-sdk alone is ~25-45 minutes.
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Names the browser resolves on its own, but Node and the Rust client do
      # not. Must precede the stack coming up (wait-ready probes them).
      - name: Resolve the *.m.localhost names
        run: |
          echo "127.0.0.1 synapse.m.localhost matrix-rtc.m.localhost app.m.localhost" \
            | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

      # Started first so image pulls and Synapse's first boot overlap the (much
      # longer) rust build.
      - name: Start the interop stack
        run: docker compose $COMPOSE_FILES up -d --wait

      # No machine-wide trust install: the suite hands the CA to the Rust peer
      # as SSL_CERT_FILE and to Node as NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS itself (see
      # interop/helpers/rust-peer.ts and playwright.config.ts, and INTEROP.md
      # for why that is enough). This step only fails loudly if the stack did
      # not produce a CA at all, which would otherwise surface much later as an
      # UnknownIssuer deep inside the peer.
      - name: Check the stack minted its dev CA
        run: test -r demo/backend/data/tls/local-ca.crt

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          # wasm32 for the web peer's bindings, alongside the host target.
          targets: wasm32-unknown-unknown

      # webrtc-sys's build script shells out to pkg-config for glib-2.0 (the
      # prebuilt linux libwebrtc links it dynamically).
      - name: Install webrtc-sys system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libglib2.0-dev

      # Same key as the E2E Call workflow: identical tree, and the matrix-sdk
      # build dominates the job either way.
      - name: Rust cache
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          shared-key: e2e-call

      - name: Build the interop peer
        run: cargo build -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --features matrix-sdk,testing --example interop_peer

      # The web peer's wasm bindings. The rust-cache step above covers the
      # cargo half of this build too.
      - name: Install wasm-pack
        run: curl https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-pack/installer/init.sh -sSf | sh

      - name: Build the wasm bindings
        run: ./web/scripts/build-bindings.sh

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      # `npm ci` once a lockfile is committed (do that on the first local run —
      # it pins @playwright/test, which is the only dependency here).
      - name: Install Playwright dependencies
        working-directory: interop
        run: |
          if [ -f package-lock.json ]; then npm ci; else npm install; fi

      # The web peer page; Playwright's webServer builds and serves it.

    name: Two-client audio call
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Generous: an uncached build of matrix-sdk alone takes ~25-45 minutes.
    # With a warm rust-cache the whole job is ~10 minutes.
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Start the backend first so image pulls and Synapse's first boot overlap
      # the (much longer) rust build.
      - name: Start MatrixRTC backend
        run: docker compose -f demo/backend/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      # matrix-rtc-livekit pulls in livekit/webrtc-sys, whose build script
      # shells out to pkg-config for glib-2.0 (the prebuilt linux libwebrtc
      # dynamically links it). Same dependency the Lint workflow installs.
      - name: Install webrtc-sys system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libglib2.0-dev

      - name: Rust cache
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          shared-key: e2e-call

      # Build without running so a compile failure is distinguishable from a
      # call failure, and the stack gets extra minutes to settle.
      - name: Build e2e test
        run: cargo test -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --features matrix-sdk,testing --test e2e_call --no-run

      - name: Wait for backend readiness
        run: ./demo/backend/wait-ready.sh

      - name: Run e2e call test
        # --test-threads=1: the scenarios share the compose stack; run them
        # sequentially.
        run: cargo test -p matrix-rtc-call-sdk --features matrix-sdk,testing --test e2e_call -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
        env:
          # `debug` on our own crates: this is the only CI job that exercises a
          # real join end to end, so its log is the reference for what a healthy
          # sequence looks like. `livekit`/`webrtc_sys` stay at `warn` — at
          # `debug` they are most of the output.
          RUST_LOG: info,matrix_rtc_core=debug,matrix_rtc_call_sdk=debug,matrix_rtc_livekit=debug,livekit=warn,webrtc_sys=warn

      # Always, not just on failure: the auth-service (lk-jwt) logs are the
      # only visibility into the OpenID/token hop, and green runs that log
      # oddities are how drift gets spotted early.
      - name: Backend logs
        if: always()
        run: docker compose -f demo/backend/docker-compose.yml logs --no-color

      # The recorded audio is the best evidence when tone detection fails.
      - name: Upload recorded audio
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: e2e-received-wav
          path: target/e2e/*.wav
          if-no-files-found: ignore

      - name: Teardown backend
        if: always()
        run: docker compose -f demo/backend/docker-compose.yml down -v

# Cuts a release of the mobile artifacts (media variant): the Android AAR to
# GitHub Packages (and Maven Central when its secrets are set) and the iOS
# xcframework as a Swift package, both attached to a GitHub Release tagged
# v<version>. See RELEASING.md for the procedure around it.
# Dispatched by hand, not on tag push: the tag is created here, after every
# artifact has been built, so a tag never exists without its assets and the
# Package.swift committed at the tag points at the zip attached to it.
# A dry run builds and uploads everything as workflow artifacts and stops
# before anything is published, committed or tagged.

name: Release

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        description: 'Version to release, e.g. 0.2.0. Must equal [workspace.package].version in Cargo.toml.'
        required: true
        type: string
      dry_run:
        description: 'Build only: no publish, commit, tag or GitHub release'
        required: true
        type: boolean
        default: true

permissions: {}

concurrency:
  group: release
  cancel-in-progress: false

env:
  MEDIA: "1"
  CARGO_PROFILE: mobile-release

jobs:
  validate:
    name: Validate ${{ inputs.version }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      - name: Version matches Cargo.toml
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
        run: |
          cargo_version="$(cargo metadata --no-deps --format-version 1 \
            | jq -r '.packages[] | select(.name == "matrix-rtc-ffi") | .version')"
          if [ "$cargo_version" != "$VERSION" ]; then
            echo "::error::Requested $VERSION but Cargo.toml says $cargo_version. Bump [workspace.package].version first."
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Tag does not exist yet
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
        run: |
          if git rev-parse -q --verify "refs/tags/v$VERSION" > /dev/null; then
            echo "::error::Tag v$VERSION already exists."
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Extract release notes from CHANGELOG.md
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
        run: |
          mkdir -p dist
          ./scripts/changelog-section.sh "$VERSION" > dist/release-notes.md
          echo "Release notes:"
          cat dist/release-notes.md

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-notes
          path: dist/release-notes.md
          if-no-files-found: error

  android:
    name: Android ${{ matrix.target }}
    needs: validate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Uncached, each target compiles the libwebrtc-carrying stack with LTO.
    timeout-minutes: 120
    strategy:
      fail-fast: true
      matrix:
        target:
          - aarch64-linux-android
          - armv7-linux-androideabi
          - x86_64-linux-android
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}

      - name: Setup Java
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 17

      - name: Install cargo-ndk
        run: cargo install cargo-ndk

      - name: Rust cache
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          shared-key: release-android-${{ matrix.target }}

      # The runner image ships the NDK under $ANDROID_HOME/ndk/<version>; the
      # build script's resolve_ndk() finds it there.
      - name: Build native library
        run: |
          ./scripts/build-android-aar.sh \
            --target "${{ matrix.target }}" \
            --profile "$CARGO_PROFILE" \
            --split-debug

      - name: Upload native library
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-lib-${{ matrix.target }}
          # The path below the first wildcard (the ABI directory) is preserved.
          path: mobile/android/matrixrtc/src/main/jniLibs/*/libmatrix_rtc_ffi.so
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7

      - name: Upload debug symbols
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-debuginfo-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: mobile/android/debuginfo/
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7

      # Identical for every ABI, so taken from one job only.
      - name: Upload Kotlin bindings
        if: matrix.target == 'aarch64-linux-android'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-kotlin
          path: mobile/android/matrixrtc/src/main/java/
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7

      - name: Upload libwebrtc.jar
        if: matrix.target == 'aarch64-linux-android'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-webrtc-jar
          path: mobile/android/matrixrtc/libs/libwebrtc.jar
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7

  ios:
    name: iOS xcframework
    needs: validate
    # macos-latest is Apple Silicon, matching the media variant's arm64-only
    # simulator support.
    runs-on: macos-latest
    timeout-minutes: 120
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: aarch64-apple-ios,aarch64-apple-ios-sim

      - name: Rust cache
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          shared-key: release-ios

      - name: Build xcframework
        run: |
          ./scripts/build-ios-xcframework.sh \
            --profile "$CARGO_PROFILE" \
            --swift-out Sources/MatrixRtc \
            --zip

      - name: Upload xcframework zip
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: ios-xcframework
          path: |
            mobile/ios/build/MatrixRtcFFI.xcframework.zip
            mobile/ios/build/MatrixRtcFFI.xcframework.zip.sha256
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7

      - name: Upload Swift sources
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: ios-swift
          path: Sources/MatrixRtc/
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7

  publish:
    name: ${{ inputs.dry_run && 'Assemble (dry run)' || 'Publish' }} v${{ inputs.version }}
    needs: [validate, android, ios]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write   # tag, release commit, GitHub Release
      packages: write   # GitHub Packages (Maven)
    env:
      VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
      # `secrets` is not allowed in a step's `if`, so the presence check is
      # evaluated here and the step tests the resulting env value.
      MAVEN_CENTRAL_CONFIGURED: ${{ secrets.MAVEN_CENTRAL_USERNAME != '' }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # The release commit (Package.swift + Sources/MatrixRtc) is pushed
          # back to the branch this run was dispatched on.
          ref: ${{ github.ref }}
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: true

      - name: Setup Java
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 17

      - name: Download native libraries
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: android-lib-*
          merge-multiple: true
          path: mobile/android/matrixrtc/src/main/jniLibs/

      - name: Download Kotlin bindings
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-kotlin
          path: mobile/android/matrixrtc/src/main/java/

      - name: Download libwebrtc.jar
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-webrtc-jar
          path: mobile/android/matrixrtc/libs/

      - name: Download debug symbols
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: android-debuginfo-*
          merge-multiple: true
          path: debuginfo/

      - name: Download xcframework zip
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: ios-xcframework
          path: dist/

      - name: Download Swift sources
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: ios-swift
          path: Sources/MatrixRtc/

      - name: Download release notes
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-notes
          path: dist/

      - name: Assemble AAR
        run: |
          ls -R mobile/android/matrixrtc/src/main/jniLibs
          ./scripts/build-android-aar.sh --skip-build --skip-codegen --version "$VERSION"
          cp mobile/android/matrixrtc/build/outputs/aar/matrixrtc-release.aar \
             "dist/matrix-rtc-android-$VERSION.aar"

      - name: Package debug symbols
        run: |
          (cd debuginfo && zip -r "../dist/matrix-rtc-android-$VERSION-debuginfo.zip" .)

      - name: Point Package.swift at the release
        run: |
          ./scripts/update-package-swift.sh "$VERSION" "$(cat dist/MatrixRtcFFI.xcframework.zip.sha256)"
          rm dist/MatrixRtcFFI.xcframework.zip.sha256
          git diff --stat

      - name: Checksums
        run: |
          (cd dist && sha256sum *.aar *.zip > SHA256SUMS && cat SHA256SUMS)

      # Always exercised, even on a dry run: it fails on a POM or signing
      # misconfiguration before anything reaches a remote repository.
      - name: Publish to the local Maven repository (POM check)
        working-directory: mobile/android
        run: |
          ./gradlew :matrixrtc:publishReleasePublicationToMavenLocal \
            -PmatrixRtcMedia=true -PmatrixRtcVersion="$VERSION"
          find ~/.m2/repository -path '*matrix-rtc-android*' -name '*.pom' -exec cat {} \;

      - name: Upload release bundle
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-v${{ inputs.version }}
          path: |
            dist/
            Package.swift
            Sources/MatrixRtc/
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 30

      - name: Publish to GitHub Packages
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        working-directory: mobile/android
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          ./gradlew :matrixrtc:publishReleasePublicationToGitHubPackagesRepository \
            -PmatrixRtcMedia=true -PmatrixRtcVersion="$VERSION"

      - name: Publish to Maven Central
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run && env.MAVEN_CENTRAL_CONFIGURED == 'true' }}
        working-directory: mobile/android
        env:
          MAVEN_CENTRAL_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.MAVEN_CENTRAL_USERNAME }}
          MAVEN_CENTRAL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MAVEN_CENTRAL_PASSWORD }}
          SIGNING_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.SIGNING_KEY_ID }}
          SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.SIGNING_KEY }}
          SIGNING_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SIGNING_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          ./gradlew publishToSonatype closeAndReleaseSonatypeStagingRepository \
            -PmatrixRtcMedia=true -PmatrixRtcVersion="$VERSION"

      - name: Commit and tag
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        run: |
          git config user.name "ElementBot"
          git config user.email "android@element.io"
          git add Package.swift Sources/MatrixRtc
          git commit -m "Release v$VERSION"
          git tag -a "v$VERSION" -m "v$VERSION"
          git push origin "HEAD:${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" "refs/tags/v$VERSION"

      - name: Create GitHub Release
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          tag_name: v${{ inputs.version }}
          name: v${{ inputs.version }}
          # A semver pre-release (0.2.0-rc.1) must not become "latest".
          prerelease: ${{ contains(inputs.version, '-') }}
          body_path: dist/release-notes.md
          files: |
            dist/matrix-rtc-android-${{ inputs.version }}.aar
            dist/matrix-rtc-android-${{ inputs.version }}-debuginfo.zip
            dist/MatrixRtcFFI.xcframework.zip
            dist/SHA256SUMS
          fail_on_unmatched_files: true

# (AAR, xcframework) built by .github/workflows/release.yml, not crates.io. The
# livekit and matrix-sdk crates could not be published anyway — they pin matrix-sdk
# by git rev, which the registry rejects.

version = "0.5.0-rc.5"
edition = "2024"
license = "AGPL-3.0-only OR LicenseRef-Element-Commercial"

# Profile of the distributed mobile artifacts (`scripts/build-*.sh --profile
# mobile-release`, used by .github/workflows/release.yml). `opt-level = "s"`
# plus LTO is what matrix-rust-sdk ships to Element X. Debug info is kept as
# line tables and not stripped here: the Android script splits it into a
# `.debug` file for symbolication and strips the shipped `.so` itself, and on
# Apple the static archive carries it into the app's dSYM.
[profile.mobile-release]
inherits = "release"
opt-level = "s"
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
debug = "line-tables-only"
strip = "none"

[workspace.dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
thiserror = "2.0"
uniffi = "0.29"
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"
wasm-bindgen-test = "0.3"
serde-wasm-bindgen = "0.6"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt", "sync"] }
tokio-stream = { version = "0.1", features = ["sync"] }
log = "0.4"
async-trait = "0.1"

# The LiveKit client and the HTTP client of the token exchange, declared once:
# `matrix-rtc-livekit` names their types in its API (a session's `RoomEvent`s,
# the token exchange's `reqwest::Client`) and `matrix-rtc-call-sdk` uses the
# same ones, so two version specs would build two copies whose types do not
# match.
reqwest = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["json", "rustls-tls"] }

# `livekit`: keep default features (notably `tokio`, which enables the signal client) and
# select the rustls TLS backend for the SFU WebSocket/HTTP connections.
#
# BOTH root stores, deliberately. `rustls-tls-native-roots` alone breaks the
# signal WebSocket on every Android device: `rustls-native-certs` probes the
# filesystem (/etc/ssl/certs, SSL_CERT_FILE, ...) and Android keeps its trust
# store in the Java KeyStore instead, so it returns zero certificates and
# tokio-tungstenite fails the connection with "no native root CA certificates
# found (errors: [])". Nothing failed to parse — there was nothing to read.
#
# tokio-tungstenite is written for the two to coexist (src/tls.rs): an empty
# native store is fatal *only* when `rustls-tls-webpki-roots` is off, and the
# webpki roots are then unioned into the same store. So Android falls back to
# the bundled roots while desktop keeps the system store, including any
# enterprise CA an admin added there.
#
# Not a swap, for two reasons. Desktop would lose user/enterprise-added CAs.
# And livekit-api gates its WSS-over-HTTP-proxy path on
# `rustls-tls-native-roots` (signal_client/signal_stream.rs) — without it, any
# wss:// through a proxy becomes a hard "requires rustls-tls-native-roots".
#
# This does NOT give Android enterprise/internal CAs: nothing here can read the
# Java KeyStore. That needs a platform verifier
# (`rustls-platform-verifier`) plumbed through livekit-api, which calls
# `connect_async` without a connector and so cannot accept one today — an
# upstream change, not a local knob.
livekit = { version = "0.7", features = [
    "rustls-tls-native-roots",
    "rustls-tls-webpki-roots",
] }

# The Matrix SDK, used by matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk, and by matrix-rtc-call-sdk behind
# its `matrix-sdk` feature. Upstream `main`, pinned to a rev so builds are
# reproducible; the three crates MUST share one rev or cargo resolves two copies
# of matrix-sdk and the `Client` one crate takes is not the one the other accepts.
# MSC4354 sticky events come from its `unstable-msc4354` feature, which our
# `matrix-sdk` features enable.
matrix-sdk = { git = "https://github.com/matrix-org/matrix-rust-sdk", rev = "c6ad52ecc09eaa36601f55effb0a48a533eb87dd" }
matrix-sdk-base = { git = "https://github.com/matrix-org/matrix-rust-sdk", rev = "c6ad52ecc09eaa36601f55effb0a48a533eb87dd" }
matrix-sdk-ui = { git = "https://github.com/matrix-org/matrix-rust-sdk", rev = "c6ad52ecc09eaa36601f55effb0a48a533eb87dd" }

# matrix-rust-sdk carries these git pins in its own `[patch]` tables. Cargo does
# NOT propagate a dependency's `[patch]` to the consuming workspace, so they are
# replicated here verbatim, or the SDK fails to build; a downstream workspace
# that depends on matrix-rtc-matrix-sdk, or -call-sdk with `matrix-sdk` on, must do the
# same. Source: matrix-org/matrix-rust-sdk@c6ad52e Cargo.toml — keep in step when
# bumping the rev above.
[patch.crates-io]
async-compat = { git = "https://github.com/element-hq/async-compat", rev = "5a27c8b290f1f1dcfc0c4ec22c464e38528aa591" }
const_panic = { git = "https://github.com/jplatte/const_panic", rev = "e0b317a9a7bde2d48a7d15b6a60d70e4a41d3b5f" }
